specPoints.text: be able to calculate mean bond enthalpies from enthalpy changes of reaction
understand the terms ‘bond enthalpy’ and ‘mean bond enthalpy’, and be able to use bond enthalpies to calculate enthalpy changes, understanding the limitations of this method

primer.text: Breaking a bond costs energy; making one pays it back. The balance between the two accounts is the overall enthalpy change. This note defines mean bond enthalpy, works the broken-minus-formed equation on real reactions, and derives a bond enthalpy from an experimental enthalpy change, then explains why the averages can mislead.

lessons.title: The bond ledger: breaking pays, forming earns
lessons.opening: Every reaction is a bond transaction: energy is paid in to break bonds and earned back when new bonds form. The overall enthalpy change is simply the ledger balance - total break costs minus total formation earnings.
keyPoints: Breaking bonds requires energy from the surroundings, so bond breaking is endothermic.
Forming bonds releases energy to the surroundings, so bond formation is exothermic.
The overall enthalpy change equals the total energy to break bonds minus the total energy released forming bonds.
Bond enthalpies apply to gases - all species must be gaseous for the ledger to work.
A negative balance means the formation earnings outweighed the break costs: exothermic.

low.restatement: Add up what it costs to snap every bond broken, add up what is earned making every new bond, and subtract earnings from costs - the balance is the reaction's enthalpy change.
low.analogy: Demolition and construction: pay the wreckers, collect from the builders, and the net spend is the enthalpy change.
low.examPointer: Write the master equation in symbols first - sum(broken) minus sum(formed) - then substitute numbers; sign errors cluster in word-first approaches.

medium.restatement: The gas-phase restriction matters because tabulated bond enthalpies are measured between free gaseous atoms; solutions and solids carry extra intermolecular terms the ledger cannot see.
medium.analogy: The ledger only audits the molecule's own accounts, not its neighbourhood fees - liquids and solids charge neighbourhood fees.
medium.examPointer: When a question gives aqueous species, expect the answer to explain why bond-enthalpy arithmetic is unreliable there.

check.stem: What energy change accompanies bond breaking?

options.text: Energy is absorbed - breaking is endothermic
options.explanation: Pulling atoms apart resists their attraction.

options.text: Energy is released - breaking is exothermic
It depends on the bond's colour

check.stem: The overall enthalpy change in bond-enthalpy terms equals:

options.text: Total energy to break bonds minus total energy released forming bonds
The average of broken and formed

check.stem: Why must all species be gaseous for bond-enthalpy calculations?

options.text: Tabulated values measure isolated gas-phase molecules
options.explanation: Extra intermolecular terms would corrupt the ledger.
They react; their enthalpy includes extra terms.

check.stem: A bond-enthalpy calculation returns -184 kJ mol^-1. What does the sign report?

options.text: Formation released more energy than breaking consumed
Breaking cost more than forming earned

options.explanation: The sign is independent of phase notation.

check.stem: Which statement about the H-Cl bond enthalpy in HCl(g) is correct?

options.text: It is the energy to split gaseous HCl into gaseous H and Cl atoms
options.explanation: Gas to gases - the definition's scope.

options.text: It is the energy to burn hydrogen chloride
It is the energy to form HCl from solid ingredients
options.explanation: Solid phases are outside the definition.

options.text: It measures the solution's pH effect

check.stem: State the overall enthalpy change in terms of bond breaking and formation.
check.modelAnswer: The overall enthalpy change equals the total energy required to break the bonds minus the total energy released when the new bonds form.

check.stem: Classify bond breaking and bond formation as endothermic or exothermic.
check.modelAnswer: Bond breaking is endothermic (energy absorbed); bond formation is exothermic (energy released).

check.stem: Explain why bond breaking always costs energy.
check.modelAnswer: A bond exists because the paired electrons sit at lower energy between the two nuclei; pulling the atoms apart must lift the pair back to the higher, free-atom state, and that lift is paid from the surroundings.

check.stem: A reaction's ledger shows 520 kJ of breaking against 700 kJ of formation. State the overall enthalpy change and its class.
check.modelAnswer: The balance is 520 - 700 = -180 kJ mol-1, exothermic, because formation outearned breaking.

lessons.title: Mean bond enthalpy and its limits
lessons.opening: Tabulated bond enthalpies are averages: the C-H value summarises methane's four bonds, ethane's six, and every other environment into one number. Averages are useful and imprecise - knowing which is which separates good answers from great ones.
keyPoints: A mean bond enthalpy averages a bond's dissociation energy across many compounds.
Methane's mean C-H enthalpy is a quarter of its total atomisation enthalpy: four identical bonds share the bill.
The average hides environment: a C-H bond costs more to break in some molecules than in others.
Averages are measured in the gas phase, so solution calculations inherit systematic error.
Mean values give approximate enthalpy changes - data-book values beat them when available.

low.restatement: One C-H number serves every molecule because it averages them all: methane's four equal bonds split their total bill into four equal shares.
low.analogy: A menu's 'average meal price' - no actual meal costs exactly that, but it predicts the bill reasonably.
low.examPointer: Define mean bond enthalpy with the word 'average' or 'mean' and the phrase 'across a range of compounds' - precision earns the mark.

medium.restatement: The averaging is the limitation's root: since each specific bond's true strength depends on its molecular neighbourhood, cycle calculations built on means drift from measured values, and the drift grows with structural complexity.
medium.analogy: Averages are shoe sizes: close enough to walk in, wrong for the marathon.
medium.examPointer: Name at least two limitations (averaging, gas phase) when asked - single-limitation answers score half.

check.stem: What is a mean bond enthalpy?

options.text: The average energy to break a named bond across a range of compounds
The energy of the strongest version of that bond
The energy released forming the bond in water
A bond's price in a data book
options.explanation: Books tabulate the average; the definition is the averaging itself.

check.stem: Methane's atomisation to C(g) + 4H(g) absorbs 1646 kJ mol^-1. What is the mean C-H bond enthalpy?

options.explanation: Four equal shares of one bill.
That is the whole bill, not one share.
That divides by twenty - wrong denominator.

check.stem: Why can the mean C-H value misprice a specific C-H bond?

options.text: The bond's true strength depends on its molecular environment
Mean values apply only at 273 K
options.explanation: The gas-phase standard applies at 298 K.

check.stem: Which calculation inherits the most systematic error from mean bond enthalpies?

options.text: Reactions in aqueous solution using gas-phase averages
options.explanation: The phase mismatch adds error on error.

options.text: Combustion reactions using tabulated combustion values

check.stem: When both a data-book reaction enthalpy and a mean-bond-enthalpy estimate exist, which is trusted and why?

options.text: The data-book value - it is measured rather than averaged
The bond estimate - bonds are fundamental

check.stem: Define mean bond enthalpy precisely.
check.modelAnswer: The mean bond enthalpy is the average energy required to break one mole of a named bond in the gas phase, averaged across a range of compounds.

check.stem: Recall the mean C-H bond enthalpy in methane given a 1646 kJ mol^-1 atomisation enthalpy.
check.modelAnswer: 1646 divided by 4 gives about 412 kJ mol^-1 for each mean C-H bond.

check.stem: Explain why the mean C-H value in methane is exactly one quarter of the atomisation enthalpy.
check.modelAnswer: Atomisation breaks all four C-H bonds to the same gaseous-atom endpoint, and methane's four bonds are equivalent, so the total bill splits evenly into four identical shares.

check.stem: Hexane's full atomisation absorbs 4158 kJ mol^-1 across six C-H bonds and five C-C bonds; using the mean C-H of 412, estimate the total C-C contribution.
check.modelAnswer: Six C-H bonds account for 6 x 412 = 2472 kJ, so the five C-C bonds carry about 4158 - 2472 = 1686 kJ, roughly 337 kJ mol^-1 per C-C bond on this average.

lessons.title: Calculations: pricing reactions and deriving bonds
lessons.opening: Two calculation directions share one ledger: price a reaction from tabulated bonds (broken minus formed), or solve the ledger backwards to derive a bond enthalpy from a measured reaction enthalpy. Both are bookkeeping - the second just hides one number.
keyPoints: The forward calculation prices a reaction: sum the bonds broken, sum the bonds formed, subtract.
Hydrogen chloride synthesis works as (+436 + 242) - 2(431) = -184 kJ mol^-1.
The reverse direction solves for an unknown bond enthalpy from a measured enthalpy change.
Ammonia's ledger derives the mean N-H bond: broken 2252, formed 2344, so each N-H costs 2344/6.
Both directions assume gaseous species and mean bond values - approximations to declare.

low.restatement: List every bond broken on the left, every bond formed on the right, multiply by their tabulated values, and subtract formed from broken - or hide one value and solve for it.
low.analogy: A receipt with one missing price: total the known lines, subtract from the bill, and the missing line prices itself.
low.examPointer: Count bonds carefully - diatomic products like HCl appear twice per equation unit, so their bond value is multiplied by two.

medium.restatement: The reverse derivation treats the ledger as an equation in one unknown: measured change plus total formed equals total broken, so isolating the unknown bond delivers the 6.10 skill of extracting mean bond enthalpies from experimental data.
medium.analogy: Auditing backwards: the bank statement (measured change) reveals the hidden transaction (the unknown bond) once every other line is priced.
medium.examPointer: Declare the approximations in writing: mean values and gas-phase assumptions - the qualification is part of the marking scheme.

check.stem: Price the reaction H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2HCl(g) given H-H = 436, Cl-Cl = 242 and H-Cl = 431 kJ mol^-1.

options.explanation: Two H-Cl bonds form per equation.
That drops one H-Cl bond from the count.

check.stem: In the HCl pricing, why does the H-Cl value multiply by two?

options.text: The equation forms two moles of HCl
options.explanation: Two bonds form, so the earning doubles.
It is a single bond counted twice across two molecules.

check.stem: Ammonia synthesis has enthalpy change -92 kJ mol^-1. Bonds broken: N-N triple (944) and 3 x H-H (436 each). What is the total bond-forming energy?

options.explanation: The earnings must exceed the costs by 92.
That subtracts when it should add.
That is the reaction change, not the formation total.

check.stem: Continuing the ammonia ledger: the mean N-H bond enthalpy is:

options.explanation: Two ammonia molecules carry six N-H bonds.
That prices per molecule, not per bond.

check.stem: Why must the qualification 'mean values, gas phase' accompany derived bond enthalpies?

options.text: Derived values inherit the averaging and phase assumptions of the method
options.explanation: Honesty about precision is part of the answer.
They are estimates built on averages.
The gas-phase assumption is the point.

check.stem: State the master equation used in both calculation directions.
check.modelAnswer: Enthalpy change = total bond energies broken - total bond energies formed, all species gaseous.

check.stem: Recall the two numbers whose ratio prices the HCl synthesis ledger.
check.modelAnswer: 678 kJ of bond breaking against 862 kJ of bond formation, giving -184 kJ mol^-1.

check.stem: Explain why the ammonia ledger divides by six when deriving the N-H bond.
check.modelAnswer: Two ammonia molecules carry six N-H bonds in total, so the pooled formation energy splits evenly across all six to price one bond.

check.stem: Derive the mean N-H bond enthalpy from the ledger: broken 2252 kJ, reaction change -92 kJ, six N-H bonds formed.
check.modelAnswer: Formed = 2252 - (-92) = 2344 kJ across six bonds, so each N-H prices at 2344 / 6 = about 391 kJ mol-1.

glossary.definition: The energy required to break one mole of a named bond in gaseous molecules.
The average bond dissociation energy for a bond type across a range of compounds.
The conversion of a substance into free gaseous atoms.

workedExample.prompt: Using mean bond enthalpies H-H = 436, Cl-Cl = 242 and H-Cl = 431 kJ mol^-1, calculate the enthalpy change of H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2HCl(g).
steps: Bonds broken: one H-H and one Cl-Cl, costing 436 + 242 = 678 kJ.
Bonds formed: two H-Cl bonds, earning 2 x 431 = 862 kJ.
The negative balance confirms formation outearned breaking.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The enthalpy change is -184 kJ mol^-1 (exothermic).
